terms.grammar: adjective and pronoun: quid aliud? what else?; nēmō alius, nobody else
evidence: Tac. Dial. 29.3: quī domī quicquam aliud loquātur
terms.comment: Latin has no separate word: “someone else” is alius, “something else” aliud. Numquid vīs aliud?, “Anything else?”, is how one takes leave in comedy (Ter. Eun. 191, Ph. 151).

evidence: Cic. de Or. 1.60: nihilne vōbīs in mentem venit, quod praetereā Crassō requīrātis? (Lewis & Short)

terms.gloss: everyone else, the rest, the others

terms.grammar: adverb; “to somewhere else” is aliō, “from somewhere else” aliunde
evidence: Tac. Germ. 19.5: quam alibī bonae lēgēs

terms.gloss: or else, but if not, otherwise
evidence: Cic. Att. 1.2.1: sīn aliter acciderit, hūmāniter ferēmus

phrases.latin: In hoc biduum, Thāis, valē. — Mī Phaedria, et tū; numquid vīs aliud?
phrases.english: Goodbye for these two days, Thais. — Phaedria dear, you too; anything else?

phrases.latin: quotum quemque inveniēs quī domī quicquam aliud loquātur?
phrases.english: how many will you find who talk about anything else at home?
if it turns out otherwise, we shall take it like sensible people

sources: Lewis & Short: alius · Lewis & Short: praeterea · Lewis & Short: ceterus · Lewis & Short: alibi · Lewis & Short: sin
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 309.
